questions.stem:
The heights, $x$ metres, of 40 children were recorded by a teacher. The results are summarised as follows
$\sum x = 58$ $\sum x^2 = 84.829$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the mean and the variance of the heights of these 40 children.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) B1: $\bar{x} = \frac{58}{40} = 1.45$
M1: for a correct expression for $\sigma^2$ (or $s^2$) (ft their mean and condone inside square root) $\sigma^2 = \frac{84.829}{40} - 1.45^2$
A1: $= 0.018225 = $ awrt $0.0182$ (Correct answer only 2/2, no fraction)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- B1 for a correct mean (accept an exact fraction)
- (NB $s^2 = 0.0186923\ldots$ awrt 0.0187)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
The teacher decided that these statistics would be more useful in centimetres.
(b) Find
(i) the mean of these heights in centimetres,
(ii) the standard deviation of these heights in centimetres.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) 1st B1ft: for new mean $= 145$ or $100\times$ their $\bar{x}$
2nd B1: for new s.d. $= $ awrt $13.5$ (accept $s = 13.6719\ldots$ or awrt 13.7)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- New mean = 145 B1ft; New $\sigma$ = 13.5 B1

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Two more children join the group. Their heights are 130 cm and 160 cm.
(c) (i) State, giving a reason, the mean height of the 42 children.
(ii) Without recalculating the standard deviation, state, giving a reason, whether the standard deviation of the heights of the 42 children will be greater than, less than or the same as the standard deviation of the heights of the group of 40 children.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c)(i) M1: for a suitable reason. May see recalculation e.g. $\frac{"145"\times 40 + 130 + 160}{42}$ (o.e.) e.g. "both 15 away from the mean" or "both same distance from the mean" or "mean of new values is 145 or the same"
A1: for 145 or 1.45 or "no change" but M1 must be seen [no further comment needed if answer matches their (b) or (a)]
(ii) M1: for a suitable reason but must have idea that the "gap" ($=15$) $> 1$ st. dev. [ft $\sigma < 15$]
A1: for stating standard deviation will be greater (o.e.) [M1 must be seen]
Calculations (you may see): e.g. $\Sigma y^2 = 84.829 + 1.3^2 + 1.6^2 = 89.079$ leading to $\sigma = \sqrt{0.01842\ldots} = 0.13575\ldots$ or $13.6$ (cm)
or $\frac{89.079}{42} = 2.1209\ldots > \frac{84.829}{40} = 2.1207\ldots$ but $\frac{\sum x}{n}$ stays the same so $\sigma$ greater
BUT M0A0 unless we see mention of 15 (cm) or 1.5 (m) being more than 1 sd
Official notes (completeness pass):
- (c)(i) Reason e.g. mean of two extra children is the same as the original mean M1; Conclusion the mean is therefore unchanged or = 145 A1
- (ii) Reason e.g. extra children more than 1 sd from mean so increased spread M1; Conclusion therefore standard deviation will increase A1

questions.stem:
Chi wanted to summarise the scores of the 39 competitors in a village quiz. He started to produce the following stem and leaf diagram
Score
$\begin{array}{c|l}1 & 1\ 5\ 8\ 9\\ 2 & 0\ 2\ 5\ 8\ 9\\ 3 & 3\ 5\ 5\ 7\ 8\ 9\ \ldots\end{array}$ Key: $2|5$ is a score of 25
He did not complete the stem and leaf diagram but instead produced the following box plot.
Chi defined an outlier as a value that is
greater than $Q_3 + 1.5\times(Q_3-Q_1)$
or
less than $Q_1 - 1.5\times(Q_3-Q_1)$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find
(i) the interquartile range
(ii) the range.
(2)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Describe, giving a reason, the skewness of the distribution of scores.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: for a suitable reason or calculation (allow longer whisker on left etc) e.g. $Q_2-Q_1 (=9) > 5(=Q_3-Q_2)$
A1: for negative skew (dep on M1 seen) "left skew" etc is A0 [Condone incorrect "9" or "5"]

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Albert and Beth asked for their scores to be checked.
Albert's score was changed from 25 to 37
Beth's score was changed from 54 to 60
(c) On the grid on page 5, draw an updated box plot. Show clearly any calculations that you used.
(7)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) B1: for new lower quartile at 35 (stated or on box plot) [$25\to 37 \Rightarrow$ new $Q_1=35$ (may be on box plot)] [$54\to 60$ (implies upper whisker now at 60) but no change to $Q_3$]
M1: for finding the new IQR ($<14$) and attempting to re-calculate for outliers [New IQR = 12 so need to re-calculate for outliers]
A1: for at least the correct lower limit of 17 seen [Outliers now $[>47+18=65$ or$] <35-18=17$]
M1: for drawing a box with only two whiskers and median at 42 (all points $\pm 0.5$ square)
A1ft: for lower quartile of "35" (changed from 33) and upper quartile unchanged at 47
A1: for only two outliers at 11 and 15 (no overlap with whisker)
A1: for lower whisker ending at 18 (or 17) and upper whisker ending at 60
Correct box plot scores all except 1st M1A1 (i.e. 5/7); this M1A1 requires some working

parts.label: d
parts.text:
Some of the competitors complained that the questions were biased towards the younger generation. The product moment correlation coefficient between the age of the competitors and their score in the quiz is $-0.187$
(d) State, giving a reason, whether or not the complaint is supported by this statistic.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) M1: The value of pmcc is small or weak correlation (o.e.) Allow e.g. "not significant" or "not relevant" or $-0.5<r<0.5$ or "not close to $-1$" but "no correlation" is M0
A1: Therefore the complaint is not supported. Dep on M1 seen. NB M1A0 is possible
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1 for comment that pmcc is "small" so little correlation (just saying < 0 is not enough)
- A1 for suggesting the complaint is not supported e.g. "little evidence to support claim"

questions.stem:
A certain disease occurs in a population in 2 mutually exclusive types.
It is difficult to diagnose people with type $A$ of the disease and there is an unknown proportion $p$ of the population with type $A$.
It is easier to diagnose people with type $B$ of the disease and it is known that 2% of the population have type $B$.
A test has been developed to help diagnose whether or not a person has the disease. The event $T$ represents a positive result on the test. After a large-scale trial of the test, the following information was obtained.
For a person with type $B$ of the disease the probability of a positive test result is 0.96
For a person who does not have the disease the probability of a positive test result is 0.05
For a person with type $A$ of the disease the probability of a positive test result is $q$

parts.label: a
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) 1st B1: for remainder of 1st column probabilities (allow use of correct $p$ so 0.82) [0.02 and $0.98-p$ correctly placed, no mixing of % and probability]
2nd B1: for remainder of 2nd column probabilities (allow use of correct $q$ so 0.68 and 0.32) [0.96 and 0.05 plus $1-q$, 0.04, 0.95 correctly placed]
In (b) or (c) if $p$ or $q$ are used as ft in M or A marks they must be probabilities

parts.label: b
parts.text:
The probability of a randomly selected person having a positive test result is 0.169
For a person with a positive test result, the probability that they do not have the disease is $\frac{41}{169}$
(b) Find the value of $p$ and the value of $q$.
(7)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: for attempt to form eq'n in $p$ and $q$ using $\mathrm{P}(T)=0.169$ [at least 2 of 3 correct prod's]
A1: for a fully correct equation in $p$ and $q$ or possibly just $q$ (using their $p$ see 3rd M1) $\mathrm{P}(T)=pq+0.02\times 0.96+(0.98-p)\times 0.05=0.169$ $\{pq-0.05p=0.1008\}$
M1: for use of a conditional prob (ratio of probabilities with num or den correct, allow ft on num) and $\frac{41}{169}$ to form an equation in $p$
A1ft: for a correct equation using values from their tree diagram $\mathrm{P}(\text{do not have disease}|T)=\frac{"(0.98-p)"\times 0.05}{0.169}=\frac{41}{169}$
A1: for solving to get $p=0.16$ (or exact equivalent)
dM1 (dep on 1st M1): for substituting their $p$ into an equation for $q$ (ft their $p$ value) e.g. $0.16q-0.16\times 0.05=0.1008$
A1: for $q=0.68$ (or exact equivalent)

parts.label: c(i)
parts.text:
A doctor is about to see a person who she knows does not have type $B$ of the disease but does have a positive test result.
(c) (i) Find the probability that this person has type $A$ of the disease.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c)(i) M1: for an attempt at a conditional prob with numerator of their $pq$ (num < denom) $\mathrm{P}(\text{type }A|T\text{ and not type }B)=\frac{pq}{pq+(0.98-p)\times 0.05}=\frac{0.1088}{0.1088+0.041}$
A1ft: for a correct ratio of probs (ft their values for $p$ or $q$ with at least one correct)
A1: $=0.7263\ldots$ awrt $0.726$ (or exact fraction $\frac{544}{749}$)

parts.label: c(ii)
parts.text:
(ii) State, giving a reason, whether or not the doctor will find the test useful.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: (c)(ii) B1: If (c)(i) $<0.7$ then B0 for suggesting test should be useful (accept "yes") plus statement about increased prob or "more likely to have type $A$ than no disease" or "prob of $A$ is high". Should find test useful, doctor knows there is a much greater chance that the person has type $A$ (0.73 compared to 0.16 or $0.163\ldots$[from $\frac{0.16}{0.98}$])

questions.stem: The weights of packages delivered to Susie are normally distributed with a mean of 510 grams and a standard deviation of 45 grams.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the probability that a randomly selected package delivered to Susie weighs less than 450 grams.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) [$W=$ weight of a package delivered to Susie $W\sim N(510,45^2)$]
M1: for standardising 450 with 510 and 45 (allow $\pm$) $\mathrm{P}(W<450)=\mathrm{P}\left(Z<\frac{450-510}{45}\right)$ or $\mathrm{P}(Z<-1.3333)$
M1: for $1-p$ where $0.90<p<0.99$ $=1-0.9082$
A1: for answer in the range 0.0912 to 0.0918 inclusive (calc. $0.09121133\ldots$) $=0.0918$
Correct answer only in (a), (c) or (d) scores all the marks for that part

parts.label: b
parts.text:
The heaviest 5% of packages delivered to Susie are delivered by Rav in his van, the others are delivered by Taruni on foot.
(b) Find the weight of the lightest package that Rav would deliver to Susie.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) [$\mathrm{P}(W>d)=0.05$ implies] M1: for standardising their letter $d$ with 510 and 45 and setting equal to $z$ value $1<|z|<2$ $\frac{d-510}{45}=1.6449$
B1: for use of $z=\pm 1.6449$ or better (calc $1.644853626\ldots$)
A1: for awrt 584 (calc $584.0184\ldots$) $d=584.0205\ldots$ awrt $\mathbf{584}$ [awrt 584.02 scores 3/3; 584 scores M1B0A1]

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Susie randomly selects a package from those delivered by Taruni.
(c) Find the probability that this package weighs more than 450 grams.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) [$\mathrm{P}(W>450|W<"584.02\ldots")=$] M1: for a correct ratio of probability expressions ft their answer to (b) where (b)$>450$ $\frac{\mathrm{P}(450<W<"584.02\ldots")}{\mathrm{P}(W<"584.02\ldots")}$
M1: for numerator of awrt $0.95-$ their answer to (a) $\frac{0.95-"0.0918"}{0.95}$ or $\frac{"0.9082"-0.05}{0.95}$
A1: for a correct denominator of awrt 0.95 (dep on M1M1). NB a correct ratio of probabilities will score the 1st 3 marks
A1: $=0.903368\ldots$ awrt $\mathbf{0.904}$ or $\mathbf{0.903}$

parts.label: d
parts.text:
On Tuesday there are 5 packages delivered to Susie.
(d) Find the probability that 4 are delivered by Taruni and 1 is delivered by Rav.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) M1: for $kp^4(1-p)$ for any positive integer $k$ and any probability $p$ (allow $k=1$) $\left(\frac{19}{20}\right)^4\times\frac{1}{20}\times 5$
dM1: for $k=5$
A1: $=0.203626\ldots$ awrt $\mathbf{0.204}$
